name: Mederma / onion extract scar gel
lead: Mederma is an over-the-counter brand of topical scar products whose best-known product, Mederma Advanced Scar Gel, contains an extract of onion bulb (Allium cepa) together with other ingredients such as allantoin. It is marketed for improving the appearance of scars from surgery, injury, burns and acne.[1] People use it on healed skin after surgery, injury or acne, aiming for scars that look flatter, softer and less red as they mature.

The brand was introduced in the United States in 1997 by Merz Pharmaceuticals and later passed to HRA Pharma (2019) and then Perrigo, according to one AI-generated encyclopedia summary.[1] Manufacturer claims of visible improvement in scar texture, colour and softness after weeks to months of daily use are described there.[1]

Published evidence is limited and mixed. A randomized, double-blind comparison of onion extract gel with a petrolatum-based emollient on new surgical scars has been published,[2] a rabbit-ear scar model study examined the product,[3] and several small trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.[4][5][6] Clinical references such as Wikipedia describe silicone, pressure, massage and steroid injection as the more commonly discussed scar treatments, and mention onion extract mainly as a comparator.[7]

paras: The flagship product is a water-based gel applied once daily to healed skin. The maker describes a three-part action of retaining moisture, supporting cell renewal and supporting collagen formation, and recommends roughly 8 weeks of use on new scars and 3 to 6 months on older ones.[1] Other products under the brand include an overnight cream, an SPF cream and a children's gel.[1]
The extract in the gel is described as containing flavonoids such as quercetin and kaempferol, which laboratory literature associates with anti-inflammatory activity.[1]

Hypertrophic scars form when collagen builds up excessively after injury that reaches the deep dermis; mechanical tension on the wound is considered a leading cause, and they can keep thickening for up to six months and typically fade over one to two years [7]. Wikipedia lists early pressure or massage, silicone gel sheeting, corticosteroid injection, laser therapy, cryosurgery and surgical revision after a year among management options, and mentions onion extract as the comparator against which silicone gel sheeting may slightly improve scar appearance [7].

A 2002 rabbit-ear study opened by noting that accepted conservative treatments for hypertrophic scars were limited to steroid injections, radiation therapy and silicone occlusive therapy, while Mederma had become prevalent in clinical use [3].

sections.h: How scars mature and what a gel is meant to do
paras: Scarring is a normal part of wound repair: fibroblasts lay down collagen that becomes dense, cross-linked and aligned in one direction, and the resulting tissue lacks the elasticity of normal skin and does not regrow sweat glands or hair follicles.[11] The contractile myofibroblasts that drive scarring generally disappear within about 30 days, but fibres continue to be reorganised for months or years, and Wikipedia notes that redness after injury is not itself a scar and usually fades over time.[11]

This slow maturation is the context for a daily-use gel. Mederma is positioned for scars that have already closed, and the manufacturer's directions describe roughly eight weeks of use on new scars and longer courses for older ones, in line with how long scars take to settle.[1] Users generally describe the goal as a scar that is lighter, flatter and softer than it would otherwise have become, and the appearance outcome people judge is visible colour and texture rather than the underlying collagen.

sections.h: Scar types and what each looks like
paras: Wikipedia distinguishes hypertrophic scars, which are raised and red on lighter skin or dark brown on darker skin and stay within the original wound; keloids, which grow beyond the wound edges, are more common in darker skin and can recur after surgical removal; and atrophic scars, which are sunken or pitted and are often linked to acne or chickenpox.[11] The brand's marketing and the registered trials concentrate on surgical, injury and hypertrophic scars, so the scar type matters when interpreting what a trial result applies to.[1][4][5]

Silicone gel and sheeting are the most commonly cited topical comparators; a Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found only weak evidence that silicone gel sheeting prevents scarring, with studies of poor quality.[11] Other measures mentioned include pressure dressings, massage (a 2012 review found weak evidence of benefit, while a 2022 scoping review reported favourable outcomes with inconsistent methods), lasers, corticosteroid injections, surgical excision and subcision.[11]

Wikipedia's scar article states that research shows onion extract (Mederma) and vitamin E to be ineffective for scars, and that vitamin E can cause contact dermatitis in up to a third of users.[11] Manufacturer materials describe visible improvements in colour, texture and softness, and a 24-patient split-scar trial found no significant difference between onion gel and a petrolatum emollient.[1][2]

Mederma is an over-the-counter gel intended for intact, healed skin and is generally described by the maker as suitable for new and old scars on the face and body.[1] As with any topical product, local irritation, itching or contact reactions to an ingredient are possible.

In a randomised, double-blinded split-scar study published in Dermatologic Surgery in 2006, 24 patients with new surgical wounds at least 4 cm long had each scar divided in two, with one half treated with onion extract gel and the other with a petrolatum-based emollient (Aquaphor), each applied three times daily for 8 weeks. Blinded investigators and the patients rated cosmetic appearance, erythema, hypertrophy, itch, burning and pain at 2, 8 and 12 weeks, with a telephone follow-up at least 11 months after surgery. The authors reported no statistically significant difference between the two treatments in any outcome [2].

A 2002 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery used four New Zealand White rabbits with 32 hypertrophic scars; half were treated with Mederma three times daily for 4 weeks. Scar hypertrophy, vascularity, inflammation and erythema did not differ significantly from controls, but dermal collagen organisation improved significantly, and the authors suggested the product might influence scar pathophysiology [3].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed 20-person trial of Mederma on post-surgical scars (started 2012) [4], a completed phase 4 randomised comparison of two topical therapies for keloids and hypertrophic scars (30 participants, started 2006) [5], and a completed 75-person study of over-the-counter scar-management products (started 2019) [6]. A 1998 commentary in Archives of Dermatology listed onion extract cream among treatments the author regarded as lacking proven efficacy for keloids [8].

In appearance-focused communities the product is mentioned as an inexpensive, widely stocked option for acne and surgical scars. The brand says it is the most recommended by doctors and pharmacists in the United States, based on surveys it cites.[1] Ownership changed from Merz to HRA Pharma in 2019 and to Perrigo thereafter.[1]

Mederma is an over-the-counter staple in pharmacies, and discussion boards for strength training and physique sport mention it for post-surgical and injury scars. A T Nation poster in 2001 described it as pricey at about 35 dollars a tube but lasting about six months, and another poster in 2008 reported using it on a knuckle wound [9][10]. Clinicians in the scar literature more often discuss silicone, pressure and steroid approaches, and onion extract appears in reviews mainly as an emerging or comparator therapy [7].

timeline.event: Launched in the US by Merz Pharmaceuticals. [1]
An Archives of Dermatology commentary lists onion extract cream among treatments the author regards as unproven. [8]

Brand sold by Merz to HRA Pharma; an OTC scar-management comparison trial begins in the same year. [1][6]

lore.intro: Mederma is discussed as a standard over-the-counter option for acne and surgical scars.[1]

claims.claim: Onion extract gel fades and softens scars
claims.believers: Users and the manufacturer report improved scar colour, texture and softness with consistent daily use over weeks to months.[1]
claims.experts: A 24-patient randomised split-scar trial found no significant difference between the onion extract gel and a petrolatum emollient on new surgical scars [2]; a rabbit-ear study found improved collagen organisation but no reduction in hypertrophy [3].

claims.claim: It works on old acne and pockmark scars
claims.believers: The maker says it can soften and smooth new and existing scars including pockmarks.[1]
claims.experts: No published trial identified here specifically tests atrophic acne scars; registered trials concern surgical, keloid and hypertrophic scars.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: Mederma works on stretch marks and old scars as well as new ones
claims.believers: Forum users have recommended it for surgical scars and stretch marks, and one poster reported it worked well on a healing knuckle wound [9][10].
claims.experts: The published split-scar trial covered new surgical scars and found no significant difference from a petrolatum ointment [2]; no trial found here tests stretch marks.

card.summary: Over-the-counter onion extract scar gel with mixed, limited trial evidence.
card.note: Trial results are mixed; scar types and study sizes vary.

quick.overview:
Mederma is a widely sold over-the-counter gel containing onion bulb extract, marketed for improving the look of surgical, injury and acne scars.
Trial evidence is limited and mixed: some studies compare it with plain emollients, and secondary sources describe both positive and null findings.
quick.mechanism: The maker describes moisturizing, cell renewal and collagen support. Laboratory literature associates onion flavonoids with anti-inflammatory activity; human mechanisms are not established.
quick.risks: It is for external use on healed skin, away from eyes and open wounds, per product labelling. No serious adverse events have been described.

chain: Gel applied daily to healed skin over a scar
Moisturising and onion-extract (Cepalin) ingredients act on the healing scar
Scar looks softer, flatter and less red-toned as it matures
angle.text: Users smooth the gel onto closed surgical, injury or acne scars once a day for weeks to months, the way the manufacturer's directions describe. The aim is a less noticeable scar, particularly on visible areas such as the face and neck.
